title.narrative: Climate Resilient Cities: Promoting adaptation and circular and inclusive urban development in Mozambique

description.narrative:
The joint proposal between UN-Habitat and FAO aims to promote resilient, circular, and inclusive urban management approaches, focusing on increasing access to services and livelihoods for vulnerable urban populations affected by climate change while reducing disaster risk in Nampula City. This initiative will serve as a model for integrated and circular climate-resilient cities, to be presented at local, national, and policy levels, contributing to the implementation of the National Urbanization Policy in Mozambique.
As an initial step, UN-Habitat will provide technical assistance to the municipal government under the project’s Planning Pillar to review and integrate planning and management instruments using the Plan Assessment Tool (PAT) for rapidly growing cities. Master Plans are crucial for regulating and directing sustainable urban development. Nampula’s PEU (Urban Structure Plan), approved in 2021, now in its implementation phase, is an example of this. These plans, which guide urbanization and list priorities for projects and infrastructure, are rarely reassessed to ensure their continued relevance or effectiveness over time. The PAT assesses the plan’s comprehensiveness, clarity, and ease of implementation, revealing its strengths and weaknesses to influence current and future city development.
The tool will use integrated criteria to evaluate plans across social, economic, spatial/physical, and environmental themes. It will also identify pilot areas in Nampula for implementing circular actions under Pillar 2, focusing on urban and peri-urban settings.
At least 50 municipal technicians from various departments will be trained in the Plan Assessment process, benefiting from on-the-job training and capacity-building sessions.
In the pre-identified areas, UN-Habitat will apply the “Ecosystem-based Adaptation” (EbA) tool, developed for conducting climate change and vulnerability assessments and planning responses. The EbA tool, tested in Mozambique through a UNEP Joint Project, will apply methods like climate vulnerability assessments, participatory hazard mapping, focus group discussions, household surveys, and shelter assessments. These activities will inform thematic action plans to address issues related to green spaces, ecological infrastructure, drainage, sanitation, water, soil degradation, and erosion.
A subsequent adaptation planning phase will follow, during which local authorities, communities, and other stakeholders will identify and prioritize adaptation options. Finally, an implementation strategy, financing mechanisms, and a monitoring framework will be developed to guide the project’s execution. At least 250 relevant government staff, 50% of whom will be women, will be engaged in the planning process and trained to implement urban management strategies for green, climate-circular development.
The Waste-wide Cities Tool will be applied in two target areas to inform actions related to urban waste management, assessing municipal solid waste (MSW) in terms of generation, collection, and management. Data will also be gathered to analyze waste management processes, recovery chains, and environmental controls in each neighborhood.
For the Urban Agro-systems component, UN-Habitat and FAO will jointly assess urban agriculture practices, land availability, and community management structures. This will include evaluating urban farming systems, cooperatives, and domestic productions to identify sustainable agricultural practices.
Under the Circular Interventions Pillar, the project will implement local climate actions to provide evidence for influencing national policies and regulations. Gender equality, youth engagement, and innovation for sustainable solutions will be cross-cutting themes. In the two target neighborhoods, urban ecosystem-based climate adaptation, enhanced waste management, and strengthened urban food systems will be piloted. At least 200 people will be trained in using nature-based solutions for urban resilience and adaptation. Clear criteria, based on socio-economic and climate vulnerability risk factors, will be used to identify the most vulnerable groups, especially women and girls, for these interventions.
To adapt urban ecosystems to climate change and improve resilience, physical improvements will be made in green public spaces, including tree planting, drainage construction, and flood risk reduction measures. The formalization of community land rights in public spaces will help protect these areas from alternative uses that could undermine ecological functions.
In waste management, the project will support informal waste recovery sector (IWRS) workers, including vulnerable groups like women, children, and people with disabilities, through technical and material support.
